title: 22. Interview: NoSQL Databases
summary: Interview Q&A for NoSQL Databases — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 NoSQL Databases interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between ACID and BASE, and why does it matter for distributed databases?
**Answer:** ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantees that after a `COMMIT`, every reader sees the new value, the transaction is isolated from others, and a crash won't lose it. BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) accepts that in a distributed system, achieving strong consistency requires consensus (Paxos, Raft, 2PC) on every write — which caps throughput and adds latency. BASE systems replicate writes asynchronously, accept writes on any replica (multi-master), and tolerate network partitions gracefully (AP in CAP). The cost is that readers may see stale data for milliseconds to seconds, and conflicts must be resolved (LWW, CRDTs, vector clocks). It matters because web-scale workloads (Netflix viewing history, Amazon shopping cart, Instagram feeds) cannot afford the latency of strong consistency per write. Modern NoSQL offers tunable consistency (Cassandra `LOCAL_QUORUM`, DynamoDB `strongly_consistent_read=true`) to get ACID-ish when needed and BASE the rest of the time.
**Visual:**
```
ACID:        COMMIT -> all replicas see new value immediately (strong)
                      + cost: consensus latency, lower throughput
BASE:        WRITE  -> async replicate -> eventually consistent
                      + cost: stale reads, conflict resolution
                      + benefit: high throughput, multi-DC writes, AP

Tunable:     pick per-operation:
             W+R > RF  => strong (Cassandra QUORUM)
             W+R <= RF => eventual (LOCAL_ONE)
```

### Q2. What are the four main NoSQL families and what problem does each solve?
**Answer:** The four families are key-value, document, wide-column, and graph. **Key-value stores** (Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB) treat all data as opaque bytes addressed by a key — `GET key`, `SET key value`. They solve sub-millisecond lookup workloads like caching, sessions, leaderboards. **Document stores** (MongoDB, Couchbase) store semi-structured JSON/BSON documents with per-document schema — optimal for CMS, user profiles, catalogs where schema varies per item. **Wide-column stores** (Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) store data in column families with partition key + clustering columns — purpose-built for time-series, IoT, write-heavy logs where you query "all events for entity X ordered by time." **Graph databases** (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) store entities as nodes and relationships as first-class edges — optimal for social networks, fraud detection, recommendation engines where relationships matter as much as entities. Each family is optimized for a specific data shape and access pattern; using the wrong one (e.g., MongoDB for a graph problem) leads to painful workarounds and poor performance.
**Visual:**
```
KV     (Redis, DynamoDB)        GET/SET key -> blob
DOC    (MongoDB, Couchbase)     JSON/BSON, schema per doc
WIDE   (Cassandra, HBase)       partition + clustering keys, time-series
GRAPH  (Neo4j, Neptune)         nodes + edges first-class

      opaque   semi-struct   time-ordered   relationships
      <----+--------+-----------+------------+----->
        KV        DOC        WIDE          GRAPH
```

### Q3. Explain the CAP theorem and how NoSQL databases make CAP trade-offs.
**Answer:** CAP theorem (Brewer, 2000) states that a distributed system can provide at most two of three guarantees during a network partition: Consistency (all readers see the same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (system operates despite network failures). Since partitions are inevitable in real networks, the practical choice is CP (consistency + partition tolerance) vs AP (availability + partition tolerance). Most NoSQL databases choose AP because web workloads prioritize availability — a social feed showing stale data is acceptable, downtime is not. Cassandra, DynamoDB, and Couchbase default to AP with tunable consistency. CP systems like MongoDB (with `writeConcern=majority` + `readConcern=majority`), HBase, and Redis Cluster reject writes during partitions to preserve consistency. The PACELC theorem extends CAP: when there's no partition (E for Else), the system trades Latency vs Consistency — Cassandra picks L (low latency, eventual), MongoDB can pick C (strong, higher latency). Modern systems let you tune per-operation: DynamoDB strongly consistent reads cost more and have higher latency; Cassandra `LOCAL_QUORUM` adds a round-trip vs `LOCAL_ONE`.
**Visual:**
```
                    C (consistency)
                    / \
                   /   \
              CP  /     \  AP
                 /       \
        P ------/---------\------ A
        (partition)       (availability)

CP: MongoDB (w:majority), HBase, Redis Cluster
    -> reject writes during partition (preserve C)
AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Couchbase
    -> accept writes, async reconcile (preserve A)
PACELC: when no Partition, choose Latency vs Consistency
        Cassandra: pick L (eventual, fast)
        MongoDB:   pick C (majority, slower)
```

### Q4. When should you choose NoSQL over a relational database?
**Answer:** Choose NoSQL when one or more of these conditions hold. First, single-node RDBMS can't handle the load — write throughput above ~50k/sec, data above ~5 TB, or geographical distribution needs. Below that, a well-tuned PostgreSQL/MySQL instance handles most workloads. Second, the data shape is naturally non-relational — time-series events (Cassandra), documents with varying schema (MongoDB), or graphs (Neo4j). Forcing these into RDBMS is painful. Third, availability matters more than consistency — a social feed showing a post 200 ms late is fine; a banking transaction showing the wrong balance is not. Fourth, schema evolves rapidly — startups with changing product where RDBMS migrations are a drag on velocity. Fifth, geo-distribution is required — DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra multi-DC for global write locality; RDBMS multi-master is harder. Do NOT use NoSQL for: financial transactions (needs ACID), complex joins and ad-hoc queries (NoSQL is terrible at these), small datasets (<1 TB, RDBMS is simpler), strong consistency required, or teams unfamiliar with the chosen NoSQL's operations.
**Visual:**
```
Use NoSQL when:                Use SQL when:
+ scale > 50k writes/sec       + financial transactions
+ data > 5 TB                  + complex joins / ad-hoc queries
+ non-relational data shape    + small dataset (<1 TB)
+ availability > consistency   + strong consistency required
+ schema evolves rapidly       + team knows RDBMS ops
+ geo-distribution             + complex transactions

  Most apps: PostgreSQL (default right answer)
  Specialized: NoSQL alongside (Redis cache, ES search)
```

### Q5. What is eventual consistency and what are its pitfalls?
**Answer:** Eventual consistency means that, after a write completes, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value — but readers may see stale data for a window (typically milliseconds to seconds). It enables high throughput (async replication, no quorum wait), multi-master writes (any replica accepts writes), and partition tolerance (writes continue during network splits). The pitfalls are real. First, stale reads — "I posted but my friend sees the old feed" is a classic NoSQL bug, requiring read-your-writes consistency (session stickiness, read quorum, or read-repair). Second, conflict resolution — concurrent writes to the same key from different replicas create conflicts resolved via LWW (loses data), CRDTs (complex but correct), vector clocks (detect but don't resolve), or application logic. Third, lost updates — read-modify-write without a transaction may lose updates; Cassandra counters and DynamoDB conditional writes mitigate. Fourth, no linearizable operations — "increment-and-read" isn't atomic; you need compare-and-set or transactions. Fifth, debugging is harder — the system's state is a moving target. Mitigations: tunable consistency (use `QUORUM` for critical reads), session tokens (DynamoDB returns a token to read your own write), and idempotent writes.
**Visual:**
```
Write to replica A:        A: x=2
                           B: x=1 (stale) <-- read here -> sees x=1
                           C: x=1 (stale)
... async replicate ...
                           A: x=2  B: x=2  C: x=2  (converged)

Pitfalls:                  Mitigations:
+ stale reads              + read-your-writes (session token)
+ conflicts (LWW loses)    + CRDTs, vector clocks
+ lost updates             + conditional writes, transactions
+ non-linearizable ops     + compare-and-set, quorum reads
```

### Q6. How do Cassandra and DynamoDB differ in their approach to NoSQL?
**Answer:** Cassandra (born at Facebook, 2008) is an open-source, self-hosted wide-column store using a peer-to-peer architecture (no master, every node equal). It uses consistent hashing for partitioning, replication factor per keyspace, and tunable consistency per query (`LOCAL_ONE`, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, `ALL`). Writes are appended to a commit log and memtable, then flushed to SSTables — write-optimized, no read-before-write. Multi-DC active-active is first-class. You manage operations: nodetool, repairs, compactions, GC. DynamoDB (Amazon, 2012) is a fully-managed service — Amazon handles partitioning, replication, HA, backups. You provision throughput (or use on-demand) and pay per request. The query model is restrictive: partition key + optional sort key, with local/global secondary indexes (cost extra, eventual consistency by default). Strongly consistent reads cost more and have lower throughput. DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region replication. Trade-off: Cassandra gives you control and lower cost at scale but operational burden; DynamoDB gives you zero ops but vendor lock-in, restrictive queries, and potential cost surprises at high throughput. Netflix runs ~500 Cassandra nodes themselves; Amazon.com's shopping cart uses DynamoDB managed.
**Visual:**
```
Cassandra                       DynamoDB
+ self-hosted                   + fully managed (AWS)
+ peer-to-peer, no master       + Amazon handles ops
+ tunable consistency/query     + restrictive query model
+ multi-DC active-active native + Global Tables (multi-region)
+ SSTables, write-optimized     + B-tree + partitioning
+ open-source, free             + pay per request, lock-in
+ Netflix, Instagram            + Amazon.com, Alexa

  Control + scale + cost  vs  Zero ops + lock-in
```

### Q7. What is "schemaless" really mean, and why is it a double-edged sword?
**Answer:** Schemaless means the database doesn't enforce a fixed schema — different documents or rows can have different fields. In MongoDB, one document can be `{name: "alice"}` and the next `{name: "bob", age: 30, tags: [...]}`. In Cassandra, rows in the same table can have different columns (sparse tables). The benefit is flexibility: schema evolves with the application, no migration downtime, heterogeneous data coexists, and rapid prototyping is easier. The double-edged part: schemaless doesn't mean schema-free — you've just moved the schema discipline into application code. Without enforcement, bad data creeps in: a field renamed in one service but not another, a missing field that breaks readers, a type change that breaks aggregations. By the time you notice, you have millions of inconsistent documents and no easy way to fix them. Best practices: validate schema in application code (Pydantic, JSON Schema), use versioned documents (`schema_version: 2`), plan migrations as application-level transforms, and add schema validation where supported (MongoDB JSON Schema validator, Cassandra static columns). The honest summary: schemaless shifts work, it doesn't eliminate it.
**Visual:**
```
Schemaless (MongoDB):
  { _id:1, name:"alice" }
  { _id:2, name:"bob", age:30 }
  { _id:3, name:"carol", tags:["x"] }
   -> DB accepts all, no enforcement

Reality: schema moves to app code
  + validate with Pydantic / JSON Schema
  + versioned: { ..., schema_version: 2 }
  + migrations become application transforms
  + bad data still happens, just harder to detect

  "Schemaless = schema is now your problem, not the DB's"
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're designing Netflix's "continue watching" feature for 200M users. Each user has a list of partially-watched titles with resume positions. Reads happen on every app open (~100k/sec); writes happen every 10 seconds during playback. What NoSQL do you choose and why?
**Answer:** Choose Cassandra. The access pattern is "all viewing events for user X ordered by time" — a textbook wide-column use case. Partition by `user_id`, cluster by `last_watched_at` desc, and you get O(1) partition lookup with sorted results. Cassandra handles 100k+ reads/sec across hundreds of nodes with linear scalability (add nodes, throughput grows). Multi-DC active-active means writes from any region replicate async — critical because Netflix runs in 3 AWS regions. Tunable consistency: `LOCAL_QUORUM` for writes (durability), `LOCAL_ONE` for reads (low latency, eventual is fine since "continue watching" tolerates 200ms staleness). No single point of failure — every node is equal. Write-optimized (SSTable append) handles the 10-second write burst per active session. DynamoDB is also viable (managed, no ops) but at Netflix's scale the cost would be enormous and the query model restrictive. Redis is too small (RAM-bound, ~5TB practical limit). HBase is overkill (Hadoop dependency). Netflix actually runs ~500 Cassandra nodes for exactly this — the real-world answer validates the design.
**Visual:**
```
Partition key: user_id    Clustering: last_watched_at DESC
+-----------+-------------------+----------+--------+
| user:42   | 2024-01-15T10:00Z | movie:7  | 00:42:13|
| user:42   | 2024-01-14T22:00Z | show:3   | 00:18:00|
| user:42   | 2024-01-13T08:00Z | movie:12 | 01:55:00|
+-----------+-------------------+----------+--------+
  Cassandra: 100k reads/s, 3 DCs, LOCAL_QUORUM writes
  Trade-off: ops burden (Netflix self-hosts ~500 nodes)
```

### Q2. Amazon's shopping cart must never go down — a 1-minute outage costs millions. The cart updates frequently (add/remove items) and is read on every page. DynamoDB or Cassandra, and how do you configure it?
**Answer:** Choose DynamoDB. The shopping cart is the canonical DynamoDB use case — Amazon literally built Dynamo (the predecessor) for this. DynamoDB provides 99.999% availability SLA for Global Tables, fully managed (no ops overhead during peak events like Prime Day), and autoscales throughput. Partition by `customer_id`, sort by `item_id`. Configuration: enable DynamoDB Global Tables across 3+ regions (us-east, us-west, eu-west) so a regional outage doesn't take down carts. Use on-demand capacity mode for spiky Prime Day traffic (no provisioning guesswork). For reads, eventual consistency is fine for "view cart" (saves cost, 2x throughput) — but use strongly consistent reads for checkout (correctness matters). For writes, use conditional writes to prevent lost updates (e.g., `attribute_not_exists(item_id)` to prevent duplicates). Trade-off: cost at extreme scale is high, and the query model is restrictive (no joins, secondary indexes cost extra). For Amazon.com's cart specifically, the consistency and ops story beats Cassandra's control. Real-world: Amazon uses DynamoDB for shopping cart, Alexa sessions, and tens of thousands of workloads — exactly this design.
**Visual:**
```
customer_id (PK) | item_id (SK) | qty | added_at
-----------------+--------------+-----+----------
cust:42          | SKU:100      | 2   | ...
cust:42          | SKU:555      | 1   | ...

DynamoDB config:
  + Global Tables (3 regions, 99.999% SLA)
  + on-demand capacity (Prime Day spikes)
  + eventual reads (view), strong reads (checkout)
  + conditional writes (prevent dupes / lost updates)
```

### Q3. Instagram wants to store user feeds — each user has a list of post IDs they've seen, with ranking scores. 2 billion users, average 1000 posts per feed, read-heavy (200k reads/sec). What NoSQL and why?
**Answer:** Choose Cassandra. The data shape is "list of (post_id, score) for user X ordered by score" — wide-column store with partition key `user_id` and clustering column `score DESC`. 2B users × 1000 posts = 2 trillion rows; Cassandra handles this scale via consistent hashing across thousands of nodes. Reads are 200k/sec — Cassandra's read path (memtable + SSTable + row cache) delivers sub-10ms p99 at this scale. Writes are infrequent (feed generation is offline/batched). Multi-DC active-active across Instagram's regions (us-east, eu-west, ap-southeast) ensures global read locality. Tunable consistency: `LOCAL_ONE` for reads (latency, eventual is fine — feed ranking is approximate anyway), `LOCAL_QUORUM` for writes. Trade-off: Cassandra's compaction strategies need tuning (Size-tiered for write-heavy, Leveled for read-heavy feeds), and operations require expertise (nodetool, repairs, GC tuning). Real-world: Instagram actually uses Cassandra for feed generation, message storage, and analytics at exactly this scale — billions of rows, multi-petabyte. Redis can't fit 2B feeds in RAM; MongoDB's sharding is less battle-tested at this scale; DynamoDB would cost a fortune.
**Visual:**
```
user_id (PK) | score (SK DESC) | post_id
-------------+-----------------+--------
user:1       | 0.95            | post:42
user:1       | 0.88            | post:18
user:1       | 0.71            | post:99

Cassandra:
  + 2B users x 1000 posts = 2T rows
  + multi-DC (us-east, eu-west, ap-SE)
  + LOCAL_ONE reads (latency), LOCAL_QUORUM writes
  + Leveled compaction (read-heavy)
  -> Instagram actually does this
```

### Q4. A startup is building a CMS where each article has different fields (blog posts have body+tags, videos have duration+url, galleries have image_list). Should they use MongoDB or PostgreSQL with JSONB?
**Answer:** Both work, but for a startup CMS, MongoDB is often the better first choice. The data is naturally document-shaped — heterogeneous articles with per-type schema, nested structures (author object, tags array, metadata). MongoDB's schemaless model lets the schema evolve as the product does — adding a `subtitle` field requires no migration. The query patterns are simple (fetch by slug, list by author, full-text search) — no complex joins. MongoDB's aggregation pipeline handles most analytics. Trade-offs: no multi-document transactions before 4.0 (now supported but with caveats), no joins (denormalize author into each article), and operational maturity is needed (replica set elections, shard balancing). PostgreSQL with JSONB is a strong alternative if the team already knows Postgres — it gives ACID, JSONB indexes (GIN), and the option of relational joins for parts that need them. The deciding factor: if 80%+ of data is document-shaped with no joins, MongoDB simplifies the model. If the data is mostly relational with occasional JSON, Postgres+JSONB avoids a second datastore. Real-world: Adobe uses MongoDB for Experience Manager CMS; many startups start with MongoDB and migrate to Postgres when relational needs grow (as Uber did with their trip schema).
**Visual:**
```
MongoDB (CMS):
  articles: [
    { type:"blog",   title:"...", body:"...", tags:[...] },
    { type:"video",  title:"...", duration:300, url:"..." },
    { type:"gallery", title:"...", images:[...] }
  ]
  + schemaless -> add fields freely
  + aggregation pipeline for analytics
  - no joins (denormalize author)

Postgres + JSONB (alternative):
  articles (id, slug, author_id FK, metadata JSONB)
  + ACID, joins for relational parts
  + GIN index on JSONB
  - mixed model adds complexity

  80%+ docs -> MongoDB    mostly relational -> Postgres
```

### Q5. WhatsApp handles 100B messages/day with sub-second delivery. They use a custom key-value store on Erlang/BEAM rather than MongoDB or Cassandra. Why might a custom KV store be the right choice?
**Answer:** A custom KV store makes sense when off-the-shelf options don't fit your specific workload — and WhatsApp's workload is extreme. They need: (1) 100B messages/day = ~1.2M writes/sec sustained, peaking much higher; (2) sub-second end-to-end delivery (low latency is critical); (3) billions of users with long-tail access patterns (some users very active, most inactive); (4) message ordering per conversation (FIFO per chat); (5) eventual deletion (messages expire after 30 days). Erlang/BEAM is purpose-built for concurrent, fault-tolerant telecom systems — millions of lightweight processes, hot code swaps, supervision trees. A custom store lets WhatsApp optimize the exact access pattern: append-only log per chat, indexed by (chat_id, message_seq). General-purpose NoSQL brings overhead: MongoDB's BSON parsing, Cassandra's SSTable compaction, DynamoDB's per-request cost. The trade-off of custom: engineering investment (WhatsApp hired Erlang experts), operational burden (you debug it), no community tooling. For most companies, this is the wrong choice — off-the-shelf NoSQL is good enough. WhatsApp's scale (and acquisition by Facebook) justified the investment. The lesson: custom is justified only when off-the-shelf truly can't meet your latency/throughput/cost targets, and you have the engineering capacity to maintain it.
**Visual:**
```
WhatsApp: 100B msg/day, sub-sec delivery, 2B users

Custom KV (Erlang/BEAM):
  + append-only log per chat_id, indexed by seq
  + millions of lightweight Erlang processes
  + hot code swaps, supervision trees
  + optimized for exactly this workload

Why not MongoDB/Cassandra?
  - overhead (BSON parse, compaction, per-req cost)
  - latency targets too tight
  - access pattern is narrow (chat log), not general

Trade-off:
  + perf, latency, cost optimized
  - engineering + ops investment
  Justified only at WhatsApp scale
```

### Q6. You're migrating a 10TB PostgreSQL analytics workload to NoSQL for horizontal scale. The queries are ad-hoc aggregations over time-series data with complex JOINs across 5 tables. Is NoSQL the right move?
**Answer:** Probably not — this is a trap scenario. NoSQL is optimized for specific access patterns, not ad-hoc queries with joins. Migrating this workload to MongoDB/Cassandra would require: (1) denormalizing all 5 tables into documents/column families (massive write amplification on update); (2) pre-computing every aggregation at write time (inflexible — new queries need new pre-computation); (3) giving up joins entirely (the 5-table JOIN becomes impossible without app-level fan-out). The right answer for ad-hoc analytics over time-series is a columnar OLAP database — ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, or Apache Druid. These are purpose-built for scans and aggregations over large datasets, with columnar compression, vectorized execution, and SQL support. If PostgreSQL is the bottleneck at 10TB, you've outgrown OLTP, not run into a NoSQL use case. ClickHouse handles petabytes of time-series at sub-second query latency; BigQuery is serverless and scales to any size. Trade-off: columnar OLAP is bad for OLTP (point inserts/updates) — keep PostgreSQL for transactional writes, replicate to ClickHouse/BigQuery for analytics. The lesson: "I need to scale" doesn't mean "I need NoSQL" — it means "I need the right tool for my access pattern," which here is OLAP, not NoSQL.
**Visual:**
```
Workload: 10TB time-series + ad-hoc aggregations + 5-table JOINs

Wrong:    NoSQL (MongoDB/Cassandra)
          - denormalize 5 tables -> write amplification
          - pre-compute aggregations -> inflexible
          - no JOINs -> app-level fan-out nightmare

Right:    Columnar OLAP (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake)
          + columnar compression (10x+)
          + vectorized scans, sub-second aggregations
          + SQL, joins supported
          + petabyte-scale

Architecture:  PostgreSQL (OLTP writes)
                  |  replicate (CDC)
                  v
                ClickHouse (OLAP analytics)
```

### Q7. Your team chose DynamoDB for a new product. Six months in, costs are $50k/month and growing. The lead engineer says "switch to Cassandra to save money." How do you evaluate this?
**Answer:** Don't switch blindly — quantify both the savings and the new costs. First, diagnose the DynamoDB bill: is it read/write capacity (provisioned too high? on-demand too expensive for steady traffic?), storage (large items? cold data still provisioned?), or secondary indexes (each GSI costs as much as another table)? Often 50%+ of DynamoDB cost is fixable: switch steady traffic to provisioned capacity with autoscaling, archive cold data to S3, drop unused GSIs, use smaller items (DynamoDB charges per 4KB read / 1KB write). Second, estimate Cassandra's true cost: 3-DC replication × N nodes × EC2 cost + EBS + cross-region bandwidth + ops engineer time (1-2 FTE at scale) + monitoring tooling. At small scale, DynamoDB is often cheaper than Cassandra once you factor ops. Third, evaluate the migration cost: rewriting queries, building CDC pipeline, training team, dual-running during migration. The decision: if DynamoDB costs >$200k/year AND the team has Cassandra expertise AND the workload is steady (not spiky, where DynamoDB's on-demand shines), migration may pay off in 12-18 months. Otherwise, optimize DynamoDB usage first. Real-world: many companies (Snapchat, Discord) have migrated off DynamoDB to Cassandra/ScyllaDB at scale — but only after the math worked.
**Visual:**
```
Decision tree:
  DynamoDB cost > $50k/mo?
    -> Optimize first:
       + provisioned + autoscaling (vs on-demand)
       + archive cold data to S3
       + drop unused GSIs
       + smaller items (per 4KB read / 1KB write)
    -> Still >$200k/yr AND team knows Cassandra
       AND workload steady?
          YES -> migrate to Cassandra/ScyllaDB
                 (3-DC EC2 + EBS + ops FTE)
          NO  -> stay on DynamoDB optimized

  Trap: ignore ops cost -> migration loses money
  Real-world: Snapchat, Discord migrated at scale
```

quiz.explanation: Eventual consistency means that, after a write completes, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value — but readers may see stale data for a window (typically milliseconds to seconds). It enables high throughput (async replication, no quorum wait), multi-master writes (any replica accepts writes), and partition tolerance (writes continue during network splits). The pitfalls are real.
